roof_pitch.rule: Roof pitch not less than 50 degrees for thatch or 45 degrees for flat tile (hard constraint c03).

variants.note: The later material, at a slightly lower minimum pitch than thatch.

roof_material.rule: Thatch of wheat straw or reed on early work, later flat clay tile.
roof_material.note: Direct quote of the long description's second paragraph and defining_characteristics item 4.

eave_condition.rule: Overhang at least 350 mm at the eave and 250 mm at the verge, substantial by comparison with the close-studded wall below it. The rain-bearing westerly elevation should be slate- or shingle-hung, or given a wider overhang.

construction_type.rule: Close-studded oak frame, posts at roughly 0.5-0.8 m centres, standing on a stone or brick soubassement of at least 400 mm above finished grade; no structural timber in contact with the ground (hard constraint c01). Clay ground plus an oak sill at grade is a ten-year building.
construction_type.note: Direct quote of constraint c01 and defining_characteristics item 1.

torchis_panel_max_width_in.note: Converted from the source's own 0.6 m clear width.

primary_cladding.rule: Panels of torchis (clay and chopped straw over riven laths) on early work, not exceeding about 0.6 m clear width; from the 17th century, brick nogging laid in herringbone or a chequer of red and vitrified black. Torchis and brick nogging belong to different centuries and must not be mixed on one elevation (soft constraint c05).
primary_cladding.note: Direct quote of defining_characteristics item 2, constraint c02, and constraint c05.

secondary_cladding.rule: The rain-bearing elevation -- always the westerly one -- is frequently hung entirely in slate or split chestnut shingle over the frame, a technique called essentage. It never appears on more than one elevation.
secondary_cladding.note: Direct quote of the long description's second paragraph and diagnostic_tells item 5 ('slate or shingle hanging on one elevation only, and always the westerly one').

foundation_expression.rule: A stone or brick soubassement of at least 400 mm above finished grade, with a drip or oversail, carries the frame clear of the ground -- always visible, never hidden by planting in an authentic example.
foundation_expression.note: Direct quote of constraint c01 and diagnostic_tells item 2.

window_grouping_rule.rule: Openings are formed by omitting whole studs and framing the resulting gap -- an opening cannot be cut through a stud, so every opening sits on the stud grid, in dense, uniform vertical striping with no accentuated bay (hard constraint c02).
window_grouping_rule.note: Direct quote of constraint c02 and proportional_system.bay_rhythm. Placed here rather than under `window_type` because the fact documented is the structural logic that positions openings, not the sash mechanism, which the node's own text never states.

variants.note: One more single-purpose building standing free in the hedged or walled enclosure, in the same close-studded frame on its own stone soubassement, one range deep -- the position outbuilding_types already gives the pressoir, the charreterie and the etable. The charreterie is a cart shed and is NOT offered here as a precedent for housing a car: it is open-fronted, unheated and undoored, and what is borrowed from it is a position in the scatter, nothing else.
Where the enclosure is loose enough, set on the far side of the yard so the car is parked outside the domestic half of the enclosure rather than beside it.

This is the corpus's own default garage answer (groupings/garage-and-hyphen.json) and this style must refuse it. Defining characteristic 6 and constraint c04 both say the Norman farmstead is dispersed and nothing is attached to anything -- depth is added by a second detached building, not by extending or linking the range. A hyphen turns the farm into the connected type the German and Flemish traditions built at the same latitude, and that contrast is the sharpest thing this style has.

A car wants a flat threshold, which is exactly the temptation c01 exists to stop: the sill must sit on a soubassement of at least 400 mm, because oak set into Auge clay at grade is a ten-year building. The garage floor drops to the vehicle, the frame does not.

c02 forms an opening by omitting whole studs and framing the gap; an opening cannot be cut through a stud. A single wide door removes so many studs at once that the close-studded striping -- the one thing that reads as Normandy from a kilometre away -- stops reading on that elevation.

attachment.value: detached: no hyphen, no shared wall, no shared roof
attachment.note: The style-specific departure from groupings/garage-and-hyphen.json, whose hyphen is the whole point of the grouping elsewhere. OQ 18, 24 Aug 2026: reclassified from `editorial` to `invented`. The two are different claims -- the schema defines editorial as 'our considered convention' and invented as 'no precedent exists' -- and `garage_strategy`'s own ontology note says in its first sentence that no historical precedent exists. A number about the garage door itself cannot be a convention drawn from tradition, because the tradition has no garage. The parameters left editorial on this slot are the ones carried from the dependency tradition rather than invented for the garage: subordination, ridge ratio, pitch match, cladding continuity.

soubassement_min.note: The figure is the style's own and is retrieved; carrying it onto a building type the tradition never built is the editorial part.

max_range_depth.note: c04's single-pile limit is stated as 6 m; 19.7 ft is that figure converted, not a new one. It happens to garage a car nose-in with room to open a door, so the vehicle cell can be genuinely single-pile like everything else in the enclosure. Two cars are got by length along the range, never by doubling the depth.

ridge_ratio_to_logis.note: Taken unchanged from the grouping's hierarchy rule. The steep 45-60 degree roof of this type makes the drop very legible, which is the point.

garage_strategy.rule: No traditional precedent exists for housing a car, and this style's answer is not the corpus's default one: the garage is authored as one more separate single-purpose building standing free in the enclosure, its own close-studded frame on its own 400 mm soubassement and one range deep, because the Norman farmstead's defining characteristic is that nothing is attached to anything and a hyphen would convert it into the connected type it exists in contrast to.

storey_height_range_ft.note: Converted from the source's own 2.1-2.5 m.

ceiling_height_rule.rule: Storey height 2.1 to 2.5 m (about 6.9-8.2 ft) -- low, dark and heavily beamed, per the long description's fourth paragraph.
ceiling_height_rule.note: Direct quote of typical_ratios, unit-converted from the source's metric figure.

floor_material.rule: Beaten earth on early work, later terracotta tomettes.
floor_material.note: Direct quote of the long description's fourth paragraph.

hearth_position.rule: A wide open hearth in a gable wall, with a bread oven bulging out behind it -- the sole heat source in a low, dark, heavily beamed room.
hearth_position.note: Direct quote of the long description's fourth paragraph.

clear_range_depth_max_ft.note: Converted from the source's own 6 m -- this node's own precise figure, tighter than the family's blended 18-23 ft band.

depth_and_pile.rule: Single-pile only: clear range depth not to exceed 6 m (about 19.7 ft). Depth is added by a second detached building in the enclosure, not by thickening the range (hard constraint c04).

variants.note: A freestanding privilege of the seigneurie -- not every farm has one.

outbuilding_types.rule: A dispersed farmstead of separate single-purpose buildings within a hedged or walled enclosure, not merged under one roof: logis, pressoir, charreterie, etable, boulangerie, and often a freestanding colombier.
outbuilding_types.note: Direct quote of the long description's third paragraph and defining_characteristics item 6.

fence_wall.rule: A hedged or walled enclosure planted with apple trees encloses the dispersed farmstead.
fence_wall.note: Direct quote of the long description's third paragraph.
